The most dangerous amplification occurs before the softmax, in the quantized QK dot-product that produces the raw attention logits. For a peaked head, the true distribution might concentrate 90%+ of probability mass on 1-2 tokens, meaning the dominant logit exceeds others by a margin of 5-15 points in FP16; INT4 with a typical per-tensor scale of ~0.5-1.0 introduces absolute errors of ±0.5-1.0 in those logits, which is enough to swap rank order between the top token and a competitor, collapsing the peaked distribution into something nearly uniform post-softmax. This is a phase-transition dynamic, not a smooth degradation — the softmax exponential means a logit error that crosses the "dominance margin" causes a discontinuous jump in output, not a proportional one. Post-softmax errors, by contrast, corrupt the weighted value aggregation roughly linearly and are partially self-correcting because the value vectors in well-trained models tend to cluster (GPTQ paper, Frantar et al. 2022, implicitly exploits this when it shows value quantization tolerates higher error than key/query quantization). This split diagnosis completely changes the correction strategy: pre-softmax errors demand per-head scale calibration tuned to preserve logit rank order — specifically protecting the margin between top-k logits rather than minimizing MSE globally — whereas post-softmax errors respond well to standard weight rounding corrections like GPTQ's Hessian-weighted update or SmoothQuant's activation migration (Xiao et al. 2022). AWQ (Lin et al. 2023) gets at this obliquely by upscaling salient weights, but it targets activation outliers broadly rather than isolating the logit-margin problem in peaked heads specifically, which is why peaked-head failures remain a residual weakness even in AWQ-quantized models.

When you tune INT4 scales to preserve top-k logit margin for peaked heads, you implicitly allocate more of the quantization range to the high-logit region, which means you're coarsening the step size everywhere else — a head that was diffuse during calibration gets a scale optimized for a dynamic range it never needed, leaving it with very few effective quantization levels in the moderate-logit region it actually uses at inference time. The pathological failure is scale ossification: at inference time, when an OOD input causes that previously-diffuse head to develop a peaked distribution, the coarse step size cannot represent the fine logit differences that determine rank order, so the head snaps to a false peaked state — confidently attending to the wrong token — rather than gracefully failing to a uniform distribution. This is worse than ordinary quantization noise because it's systematically directional: the error doesn't average out across sequence positions, it locks onto whatever token the coarse grid happens to favor, producing coherent but wrong attention patterns. Empirically this resembles the "attention sink" pathology documented in StreamingLLM (Xiao et al. 2023), where certain tokens attract disproportionate attention mass, but here the sink is an artifact of quantization grid alignment rather than a learned positional bias. The calibration dataset dependency makes this especially insidious — LLaMA-based models quantized with GPTQ on C4 (a common default) show measurably higher perplexity degradation on code or structured data not because those domains have harder content, but because the head-scale distribution learned from natural prose fails to cover the sharper, more syntactically-driven attention patterns code requires. The correction this implies is dynamic rescaling — something like per-token or per-sequence scale adjustment at inference time — but that breaks the static INT4 promise and reintroduces the memory and compute overhead you were trying to eliminate, which is why no major production quantization scheme has cleanly solved this tradeoff.

GPU warps execute in lockstep across 32 threads, so if even one head in a warp's assigned work triggers FP16 fallback, the entire warp stalls or serializes — meaning a layer where 10% of heads trigger fallback can run slower than a layer where 100% trigger it, because the latter at least allows a uniform FP16 kernel dispatch while the former forces the mixed-precision branching penalty on every warp that touches a triggering head. Empirically, FlexGen (Sheng et al. 2023) and subsequent disaggregated inference work show that non-uniform precision across a batch dimension causes effective throughput to track the worst element in the batch, not the average — a single sequence in a batch of 32 that triggers constant fallback in layers 15-20 can cut overall token throughput by 30-40% relative to homogeneous precision. The practical escape is to move the fallback decision from per-head-per-token to per-layer-per-batch: at the start of each layer, compute the maximum logit margin across all heads and all sequences in the batch, and if it exceeds τ, dispatch the entire layer in FP16; otherwise run full INT4. This coarsens the granularity — you lose the savings on layers that only have one triggering head — but it eliminates warp divergence entirely by ensuring every thread in every warp executes the same precision path. The cost is that high-traffic layers (typically middle layers 15-25 in LLaMA-class models, which show the highest attention entropy variance empirically) may permanently fall back to FP16, effectively giving you a hybrid-precision model that resembles what SpQR (Dettmers et al. 2023) achieves through static sensitivity analysis rather than dynamic detection. The uncomfortable arithmetic is that if 20% of layers fall back permanently, your effective bit-width rises from 4 to roughly 4.8 bits average, and at that point the memory bandwidth advantage over INT8 shrinks to the point where you need to carefully re-benchmark whether the whole scheme beats a well-tuned INT8 baseline — which for many serving configurations, it does not.

The principled tool here is layerwise relevance propagation (LRP) or activation patching: you corrupt a middle layer's attention output (simulating INT4 error), then measure how much the final logit distribution shifts, and compare that to corrupting a late layer by the same amount — if middle-layer corruption produces smaller final-logit delta than late-layer corruption of equal magnitude, the residual stream is indeed self-correcting that error. Mechanistic interpretability work, particularly from Anthropic's circuit-level studies and Meng et al.'s ROME (2022), shows that middle layers in GPT-class models perform associative recall and feature binding that is self-correcting in the sense that the same information is redundantly encoded across multiple heads — but this redundancy is precisely what makes those layers look entangled, and it means a quantization error that corrupts one head's contribution may be absorbed by sibling heads carrying the same signal. However, the self-correction argument breaks down specifically for rare or high-specificity tokens — named entities, low-frequency syntactic constructions, code identifiers — where the redundancy is thin and a single head may be the sole carrier of a critical feature, meaning the residual stream has nothing to absorb the loss with. A practical proxy for measuring whether fallback is earning its cost is to run a calibration sweep comparing perplexity on a held-out set with and without FP16 fallback in each layer independently, which takes O(n_layers) forward passes and directly measures the quality delta per layer; Frantar and Alistarh's GPTQ codebase makes this straightforward to instrument. The result of such sweeps — reported informally in several quantization ablation studies including the QuIP# work (Tseng et al. 2024) — is that fallback in the final 25% of layers recovers the most perplexity per FP16 byte spent, while middle-layer fallback often shows surprisingly flat returns, suggesting the self-correction hypothesis has real empirical support. The implication is brutal: a static policy of running middle layers in INT4 and only falling back in late layers may outperform the dynamic logit-margin scheme in both efficiency and quality, meaning the entire adaptive detection architecture may be solving the wrong problem.

The anti-correlation hypothesis is largely correct and represents a fundamental flaw in magnitude-based sorting: high activation magnitude in middle layers is often a symptom of feature binding and redundant encoding — exactly the regime where self-correction is strongest — while late-layer heads tend to have lower activation magnitudes because they're performing precise logit attribution and output projection where the representations are already sparse and non-redundant. SpQR's sensitivity scores (Dettmers et al. 2023) gesture at this when they show that the highest-impact weights for perplexity are not the largest-magnitude ones but those with high Hessian curvature — meaning small perturbations produce large output changes — which disproportionately concentrates in late layers where the loss landscape is steep. The correct sorting criterion is therefore output sensitivity, formally the diagonal of the Fisher information matrix or a cheap proxy like the squared gradient of the loss with respect to each head's output on a calibration set — this directly measures how much final perplexity moves per unit of quantization error at each head, which is the quantity you actually care about. A further refinement is counterfactual redundancy weighting: for each head, measure how much perplexity degrades when that head alone is ablated (zeroed out), and divide sensitivity by redundancy — heads with high sensitivity and low redundancy are the ones that need precision budget, and these cluster in late layers handling output-adjacent computations. Concretely, in LLaMA-2 70B, ablation studies show that heads in layers 60-80 handling positional and syntactic finalization are roughly 4-6x more sensitive per unit of activation magnitude than middle-layer heads, meaning magnitude sorting misranks them by that factor. The practical upshot is that the entire framing of this problem — sort by activation magnitude, protect the big ones — should be inverted to: sort by loss-gradient sensitivity divided by redundancy, which requires one calibration forward-backward pass per head but produces an allocation that matches where FP16 bytes actually recover quality.

response:
The sensitivity estimate computed on an INT4-quantized model is systematically biased, and the bias is worst precisely for the heads that matter most: the straight-through estimator (STE) used to approximate gradients through the quantization step function replaces the true zero gradient at non-differentiable points with 1.0, which means gradient magnitude through a saturated or clipped INT4 weight is artifically inflated, making high-error heads appear more sensitive than they are and corrupting the Fisher diagonal in exactly the high-curvature late-layer regime you care about. This is not a small perturbation — Nagel et al.'s ADAROUND (2020) explicitly documents that STE gradients in INT4 can differ from true finite-difference sensitivity estimates by factors of 2-5x for weights near quantization boundaries, and late-layer projection weights with sparse activation patterns hit boundaries more frequently than middle-layer weights with smoother distributions. The cleanest solution is to compute sensitivity on the fp16 shadow model — keeping a full-precision copy solely for calibration backward passes — which is what GPTQ implicitly does by computing its Hessian on unquantized activations, but this requires holding both INT4 and FP16 weights in memory simultaneously during calibration, doubling the memory footprint at exactly the moment you're trying to save it. A cheaper alternative is perturbation-based sensitivity without backprop: for each head, directly measure perplexity delta when that head's weights are randomly perturbed by ±1 INT4 step on the calibration set, approximating the Fisher diagonal via finite differences entirely in the forward pass; this avoids STE bias at the cost of O(n_heads) additional forward passes, which for LLaMA-3 70B is several hundred passes but remains feasible offline. The deeper problem is that INT4 quantization changes the model's functional form enough that sensitivity measured on the quantized model reflects the quantized model's loss landscape, not the FP16 model's — and since your goal is to recover FP16 quality, you want gradients from the FP16 landscape, making the FP16 shadow approach not just cleaner but arguably the only theoretically correct one. QuIP# (Tseng et al. 2024) sidesteps this partially by using incoherence preprocessing to make the quantized and unquantized loss landscapes more similar, which reduces the shadow-vs-quantized sensitivity discrepancy, but this is a mitigation rather than a solution and its effectiveness varies significantly across layer types.
